newsitem.title: USA: Spy case harm to CIA contacts "manageable"- Deutch.
newsitem.headline: Spy case harm to CIA contacts "manageable"- Deutch.

text.p: CIA Director John Deutch said on Wednesday he saw no "great jeopardy" to U.S. and foreign business people who may have been compromised by an alleged CIA double agent charged with spying for Moscow.

But he acknowledged the case of Harold Nicholson, the former CIA station chief arrested on Saturday, had a "pronouncedly negative effect" on morale at the agency, which was still assessing secrets he allegedly passed to Russia.

"I don't think that business is at any great jeopardy here," Deutch told CNN in the latest of a series of joint appearances with FBI Director Louis Freeh to report on the case. "I think that this will be quite easily managed for U.S. business and other businesses."

According to an FBI affidavit in the case, Nicholson may have given Moscow information about the Central Intelligence Agency's "access agents," private citizens such as businessmen who voluntarily share information with the government.
"The identity of these agents is classified, as they could be the target of reprisals if foreign countries were aware of their intelligence gathering activities," the affidavit said.

A search of Nicholson's van turned up a computer disk containing summaries of "access agent" briefings on topics such as the Russian banking system, efforts of a foreign country to obtain Russian missile technology, high-frequency radar research and information on the Russian economy.
The "access agents" were identified in the computer files by CIA codenames, positions and access to particular information, the affidavit said.
Current and former intelligence professionals warned that the possible disclosure of such information to Moscow would have a chilling effect on business willingness to cooperate with the CIA.

"People are going to be a little bit leery of playing closely with Uncle Sam because they fear that there might be another mole hidden there (inside the CIA)," said David Whipple, a 35-year veteran of the CIA's operations directorate who is now executive director of the Association of Former Intelligence Officers.

Whipple, a former CIA station chief in Asia, Africa and Europe, told Reuters that even before Nicholson's arrest he had been flooded by telephone calls from companies fearful that their employees could get caught in the U.S.-Russian tangle over the FBI's Oct. 29 arrest of Vladimir Galkin, a retired KGB intelligence official.

Last week, Deutch persuaded the Justice Department to release Galkin, who managed a KGB Cold War effort to steal U.S. "Star Wars" missile secrets, after Russia threatened to respond to his arrest by jailing former U.S. spies now doing business in Russia.

Deutch predicted the CIA would continue to enjoy "a good deal of success" in obtaining the voluntary cooperation of U.S. citizens who travel abroad. Asked whether the Nicholson case had had a devastating impact on morale at the CIA, he said, "I think there's no question about it."

Nicholson, charged with conspiracy to commit espionage for Moscow, will plead not guilty and seek pre-trial release from jail, his court-appointed lawyer, Jonathan Shapiro, said on Wednesday before a pre-trial hearing. The 46-year-old divored father of three was said by Shapiro to be "distressed" about his separation from his children.

The government has accused Nicholson of giving away the identities of undercover CIA officers and informants, along with an unknown quantity of other secrets, for at least the past two years, for at least $120,000 in cash payments.
